devlin2019.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
devlin2019.abstract: We introduce BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of NLP tasks without substantial task-specific architecture modifications.
devlin2019.full_text:
ABSTRACT: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.

INTRODUCTION: Language model pre-training has been shown to be effective for improving many natural language processing tasks. These include sentence-level tasks such as natural language inference and paraphrasing, as well as token-level tasks such as named entity recognition and question answering.

MODEL ARCHITECTURE: BERT uses a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder based on the original implementation described in Vaswani et al. (2017). The number of layers (Transformer blocks) is denoted as L, the hidden size as H, and the number of self-attention heads as A.

RESULTS: Table 1 shows results on the GLUE benchmark. BERT-Large achieves a score of 93.2% on the overall GLUE benchmark, establishing a new state-of-the-art across all tasks. BERT-Base achieves 84.6%. This represents a 7.7% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art.

CONCLUSION: We have introduced BERT and shown its effectiveness for a wide range of NLP tasks through extensive experiments on eleven NLP benchmarks.

brown2020.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
brown2020.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks and benchmarks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. We show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with fine-tuning. Specifically, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters.
brown2020.full_text:
ABSTRACT: We train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters — 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model — and test its performance in the few-shot setting.

INTRODUCTION: We demonstrate that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with prior state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches.

MODEL: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters. It uses the same architecture as GPT-2, including the modified initialization, pre-normalization, and reversible tokenization described therein, with the exception that we use alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention patterns in the layers of the transformer. GPT-3 was trained on a mix of datasets: Common Crawl (filtered), WebText2, Books1, Books2, and Wikipedia (English).

RESULTS: GPT-3 achieves strong results on many NLP datasets in the few-shot setting, often matching or exceeding the prior state-of-the-art without task-specific fine-tuning. On the SuperGLUE benchmark, GPT-3 one-shot performance is 71.8%, and few-shot is 76.4%.

CONCLUSION: Scaling language models to 175 billion parameters significantly improves the few-shot learning ability of models across a wide range of NLP tasks.

vaswani2017.title: Attention Is All You Need
vaswani2017.abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
vaswani2017.full_text:
ABSTRACT: We propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output.

INTRODUCTION: Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states h_t as a function of the previous hidden state h_{t-1} and the input for position t. This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples.

MODEL ARCHITECTURE: The Transformer follows an encoder-decoder structure using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder. Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. The encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations to a sequence of continuous representations. Given z, the decoder then generates an output sequence of symbols one element at a time.

SELF-ATTENTION: The Transformer uses self-attention in each of its layers. A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

RESULTS: On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, the big Transformer model outperforms the best previously reported models including ensembles by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our big model achieves a BLEU score of 41.0.

CONCLUSION: We presented the Transformer, the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output.

he2016.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
he2016.abstract: Deeper neural networks are more difficult to train. We present a residual learning framework to ease the training of networks that are substantially deeper than those used previously. We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions.
he2016.full_text:
ABSTRACT: We present a residual learning framework to ease the training of networks that are substantially deeper than those used previously. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence showing that these residual networks are easier to optimize, and can gain accuracy from considerably increased depth.

INTRODUCTION: Driven by the significance of depth, a question arises: Is learning better networks as easy as stacking more layers? An obstacle to answering this question is the notorious problem of vanishing/exploding gradients.

RESIDUAL LEARNING: Instead of hoping each few stacked layers directly fit a desired underlying mapping, we explicitly let these layers fit a residual mapping. Formally, denoting the desired underlying mapping as H(x), we let the stacked nonlinear layers fit another mapping of F(x) := H(x) − x.

RESULTS: We evaluate our method on the ImageNet 2015 Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC 2015). Our 152-layer residual network achieves 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set, winning the 1st place on the ILSVRC 2015 classification task. Note: the exact number is 3.57%, not 3.6%.

CONCLUSION: Residual networks are easier to optimize and can easily enjoy accuracy gains from greatly increased depth, producing results that are substantially better on the ImageNet, COCO object detection, and other recognition datasets.

srivastava2014.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting
srivastava2014.abstract: Deep neural nets with a large number of parameters are very powerful machine learning systems. However, overfitting is a serious problem in such networks. Large networks are also slow to use, making it difficult to deal with overfitting by combining the predictions of many different large neural nets at test time. Dropout is a technique for addressing this problem.
srivastava2014.full_text:
ABSTRACT: We introduce the dropout technique for preventing overfitting in neural networks. With dropout, we randomly drop units (along with their connections) from the neural network during training.

INTRODUCTION: Deep neural networks can be very powerful, but overfitting is a key challenge. A neural network with a large number of parameters is a very expressive model. Dropout is a regularization technique that prevents units from co-adapting too much.

METHOD: The key idea is to randomly drop units (along with their connections) from the neural network during training. This prevents units from co-adapting too much. At test time, it is easy to approximate the effect of averaging the predictions of all these thinned networks by simply using a single unthinned network that has smaller weights. This effectively combines a very large number of different neural network architectures efficiently.

FORMALLY: Consider a neural network with L hidden layers. Let z^(l) denote the vector of inputs to layer l, y^(l) denote the vector of outputs from layer l, W^(l) and b^(l) denote the weights and biases at layer l. With dropout, the feed-forward operation becomes: r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), y^(l) = r^(l) * y^(l), z_i^(l+1) = w_i^(l+1) * y^(l) + b_i^(l+1).

RESULTS: Dropout improves the performance of neural networks on supervised learning tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. On the MNIST dataset, dropout achieves a test error rate of 0.95%, while the best result without regularization is 1.60%.

CONCLUSION: Dropout is a simple but highly effective regularization technique. Randomly dropping units from a neural network during training prevents overfitting and gives significant improvements over other regularization methods.

ground_truth.reasoning: The paper explicitly states 'BERT-Large achieves a score of 93.2% on the overall GLUE benchmark' in the Results section. The claim is an exact match.
The paper clearly states GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, not over 200 billion. The claim is a factual overclaim not supported by the citation.
The paper explicitly describes the Transformer as 'relying entirely on an attention mechanism' and details multi-head self-attention in the Model Architecture section. The claim is fully supported.
The paper reports 3.57% top-5 error, not 3.6%. The claim rounds up. This is extremely close (rounding difference) so mostly supported but not perfectly exact.
The paper clearly states 'we randomly drop units from the neural network during training' and confirms this prevents overfitting. The claim is fully supported.
